3.  Cross Channel Wharfage Ordinance
  This ordinance was introduced and all further readings were waved at the April 15, 2025
  regular City Council meeting. The current costs of operating and improving the City’s
  Harbor Facilities exceeds the fees generated by the Harbor Use and Wharfage Fees. At
  the March 12, 2025 City Council Meeting, City Staff recommended extending the existing
  $0.50 cross channel wharfage fee which is scheduled to sunset on June 30, 2025.
  Additionally, City Staff recommended increasing the cross channel wharfage rate by an
  additional $2.00 on cross channel carriers departing the Avalon Harbor area.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt an ordinance repealing and replacing chapter 10-2.402(a) of the Avalon Municipal
  Code, use fees for harbor cross channel passengers, and adoption of findings under the
  California Environmental Quality Act.

4.  Final Parcel Map for Subdivision of 110 Chimes Tower Road (PC#2836)
  On May 17, 2023, the Avalon Planning Commission approved a tentative parcel map and
  coastal development permit for subdivision of the property at 110 Chimes Tower Road
  from one to two parcels (PC#2836). The project subdivides an existing 8,079 SF parcel
  into two new parcels. Parcel A is 5,773 SF and includes the existing single-family
  residence. Parcel B is 2,307 SF, inclusive of the vacant land on the west side of the
  property.
  Recommended Action
  Approve final Parcel Map No. 084192 for the subdivision of the existing parcel located at
  110 Chimes Tower Road into two new parcels.

PUBLIC HEARING

5.  Conduct a Public Hearing and Adopt a Resolution Declaring Intent to Award Medical
  Cannabis Delivers’ Permit to Catalina Cannabis, LLC.
  Pursuant to the Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) Section 5-20.070 and Resolution No. 18-
  07, an application period for parties interested in the City of Avalon’s Medical Cannabis
  Delivery Business Permit opened January 24, 2025. The City of Avalon received one
  complete application by the stated deadline from Catalina Cannabis, LLC.
  Recommended Action
  1. Open Public Hearing. 2. Hear comments from the public and applicants. 3. Close public
  hearing. 4. Per the City Manager’s recommendation, adopt a resolution declaring intent
  to award Medical Cannabis Delivery permit to Catalina Cannabis, LLC.

GENERAL BUSINESS

6.  Circuit Contract Amendment for COAST Program
  In the Fiscal Year 2024-25 Budget, City Staff included $60,000 in the general fund to
  purchase a new GEM to add to the public transit fleet. In lieu of purchasing a new vehicle,
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
MAY 6, 2025

  City Staff propose leasing up to two GEM vehicles from Circuit for $1,800 a month for a
  total, not to exceed, annual sum of $50000.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize City Staff to negotiate and execute the First Amendment to the Professional
  Ser-vices Agreement between the City of Avalon and Circuit Transit, Inc. for an additional
  not-to-exceed annual sum of $50,000.

7.  Change Order for Cultural Resources Consultation Agreement with Montrose
  Environmental Services
  On April 17, 2025, Montrose provided City Staff with Change Order #1. This change order
  request expands Montrose’s monitoring time for the Five Corners Site Improvement
  Project until May 2025. Initially, monitoring efforts were projected to continue from
  December 2024 through the end of March 2025. However, due to an expanded project
  schedule, and cultural findings within the project area, Montrose and City Staff see the
  need to expand the site monitoring through May 2025.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to execute a change order for the professional services
  agreement with Montrose Environmental Solutions, Inc., to continue to provide cultural
  resource consulting for the Five Corner Site Improvement Project, for an additional sum
  of $47,466 for a new total contract sum of $165,355.

8.  Civic Center Housing Proiect Phase I Award
  On December 17, 2024 City Council authorized the issuance of a Request for Proposal
  for the Civic Center Housing Project, a proposed complex located adjacent to City Hall.
  On March 3, 2025 the RFP closed and City staff received a total three proposals.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to execute an agreement with US Offsite for the Civic Center
  Housing Project Phase 1 in an amount not-to-exceed $55,000.

9.  Contract Award to International Consulting Services, Inc. for On-Call Consulting Services
  At this time, International Consulting Services, Inc. (ICS) works as a sub-consultant for
  ESG, Engineering, Inc (ESG). ICS performs high level project management support for
  the Workforce Housing and Cabrillo Mole Rehabilitation Phase II Projects as a sub-
  consultant. By contracting directly with ICS, the City anticipates a significant cost savings
  from the mark-up provided for their services when contracted through ESG.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to execute an agreement with International Consulting
  Services, Inc. to provide on-call project management services in an amount not-to-exceed
  $1 00,000 annually for an initial three-year term.

10.  Approval of Professional Services Agreement with N2W Engineering to Prepare a Climate
  Change Plan
  As part of its regulatory obligations under the NPDES municipal stormwater permit, the
  City of Avalon is required to implement planning measures addressing climate change

  impacts related to water quality, stormwater runoff, sea-level rise, and long-term
  environmental resilience.
  Recommended Action
  Per the City’s procurement policy, authorize the City Manager or designee, to execute an
  agreement with N2W Engineering to provide professional services for the development
  of a Climate Change Plan for the City of Avalon. The Climate Change Plan is an NPDES
  permit requirement.

SUBJECT:  Cross Channel Wharfage Ordinance

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Adopt an ordinance repealing and replacing chapter 10-
2.402(a) of the Avalon Municipal Code, use fees for harbor cross channel passengers, and
adoption of findings under the California Environmental Quality Act.

REPORT SUMMARY: This ordinance was introduced, and all further readings were waived at
the April 15, 2025 regular City Council Meeting.

The current costs of operating the City’s Harbor Facilities and scheduled upgrades of those
facilities exceed the fees generated by the Harbor Use and Wharfage Fees. At the March 12,
2025 City Council Meeting, City Staff recommended extending the existing $0.50 cross
channel wharfage fee which is scheduled to sunset on June 30, 2025. Additionally, City Staff
recommended increasing the cross channel wharfage rate by an additional $2.00 on cross
channel carriers departing the Avalon Harbor area, from $3.00 to $5.00. City Staff prepared an
analysis of its operations to determine the per passenger cross channel wharfage fee that
would reimburse the City’s Harbor Fund on a cost-based and proportional basis. The proposed
fee increases are required to adequately fund the cross channel passenger’s share of
operations and planned capital outlays in the harbor as outlined in the analysis, which has
been included as an attachment to this report.

The proposed application of the fee on departures only is to balance the current $2.00
Measure H special tax assessed on arrivals and would result in a total cost imposed by the
City of $10.00 round-trip ($8.00 for Cross Channel Wharfage and $2.00 Measure H Special
Tax). When the Measure H Special Tax ceases to be imposed, the City could reduce or modify
the fees increased herein, if the fiscal situation merits such a reduction.

The proposed $2.00 increase would generate an additional $1 .30 million in new cross-channel
wharfage revenues dedicated to fund capital projects. Based on prior discussions with cross
channel operators, City Staff proposes implementing the wharfage increase effective
September 2, 2025 to provide operators with adequate notice in consideration for existing
advertisements and bookings under the current rate.

Effective thirty (30) days after the adoption of the ordinance, City Staff is proposing to charge
all boats, ships, vessels, airplanes or other transportation facilities carrying passengers for hire
or charter, whether operating under the authority of the California Public Utilities Commission
 or not, which land, discharge, load, or embark passengers on, to, or from such City harbor
facilities, $3.00 for each passenger so landed, discharged, loaded or embarked. The effect of
this would be to extend to $50 fee scheduled to end on June 30, 2025.

Effective September 2, 2025, City Staff is proposing to charge all boats, ships, vessels,
airplanes or other transportation facilities carrying passengers for hire or charter, whether
operating under the authority of the California Public Utilities Commission or not, which land,
discharge, load, or embark passengers on, to, or from such City harbor facilities, $3.00 for
each passenger so landed, discharged, and $5.00 for each passenger so loaded or embarked.

City Staff further recommends conducting a review of use rates on a periodic basis to ensure
the Harbor Fund is reimbursed by its users on a cost-based and proportional basis.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The Avalon Municipal
Code will not be amended and the cross channel wharfage will remain $3.00 per passenger
until June 30, 2025 and be reduced by $0.50 per passenger beginning July 1, 2025. City would
not have sufficient revenues in the Harbor Fund to fund planned capital outlays and Harbor
operations, including the second phase of the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal Rehabilitation
Project.

SUBJECT:  Cross Channel Wharfage Rate Analysis

DATE:  March 26, 2025

Summary: The current cross channel wharfage rate of $6.00 per passenger round-trip is
sufficient to cover the proportional share of operating costs; however, cross channel
should be increased be increased by up to $3.25 per passenger, rounding to the nearest
$0.25, to cover the proportional share of capital expenditures based on the current capital
budget.

Background: The Harbor Fund is an enterprise fund and the costs associated with harbor
operations and the maintenance of harbor infrastructure should be recouped through
various charges on users of harbor facilities. The cost to operate the harbor increases
annually and revenues need to grow to cover these increased costs. The majority of harbor
revenues are collected from wharfage fees which are charged to cross-channel and cruise
ship operators on a per passenger basis. Unlike other harbor use fees that are assessed
as a percentage of the operator’s gross receipts or are subject to annual increases through
the miscellaneous fee schedule (e.g. nightly mooring rates), wharfage fees have not been
scheduled to increase annually in recent years, requiring annual increases in the number
of passengers in order to grow the revenues necessary to recoup the annual increased
operating costs.

On December 4, 2018, the City Council amended the Avalon Municipal Code increasing
the cross channel wharfage by $0.50 in each direction ($1.00 round trip) with the new
revenues dedicated exclusively to capital improvements in the harbor. Prior to March 1,
2019, the City had assessed a $2.50 per passenger charge ($5.00 round trip) with 75% of
wharfage revenues collected to fund harbor operations and 25% to fund capital
improvements. The increase was initially scheduled to sunset in February 2021 and was
subsequently extended through June 30, 2025. The increase has raised $3.58 million in
additional harbor revenues since its inception through December 31, 2024.

The revenue increase was initially required to fund the local match for the first phase of
the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal rehabilitation estimated at a cost of $2.65 million at the
time the rate increase was adopted. The first phase was completed in the fiscal year ended
June 30, 2021 for a total project cost of $5.11 million ($2.71 net of grants received). Other
projects identified in the initial staff report to support the rate increase include the second
phase of the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal rehabilitation with project spending to date of

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Approve final Parcel Map No. 084192 for the subdivision
of the existing parcel located at 110 Chimes Tower Road into two new parcels.

REPORT SUMMARY: Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) Chapter 9-2 sets forth regulations
for the division and mapping of land. Subject to the amendments, deletions, and additions
set forth in this chapter, the City has adopted Los Angeles County Subdivision Ordinance
No. 4478, as amended and in effect on April 7, 1975, as the Subdivision Ordinance of the
City. Furthermore, all divisions of land must comply with the provisions of the Subdivision
Map Act.

On May 17, 2023, the Avalon Planning Commission approved a tentative parcel map and
coastal development permit for subdivision of the property at 110 Chimes Tower Road
from one to two parcels (PC#2836). The project subdivides an existing 8,079 SF parcel
into two new parcels. Parcel A is 5,773 SF and includes the existing single-family
residence. Parcel B is 2,307 SF, inclusive of the vacant land on the west side of the
property.

In approving the tentative parcel map, the Planning Commission took into consideration
that the proposed subdivision met the requirements of the AMC for lots located in the
Multiple Residential, High Density (HD) zone, and that adequate facilities, such as streets
and utilities, exist in the project area to serve the basic infrastructure needs of the lots so
created.

The Planning Commission determined that the project qualified for streamlined review
under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) per State CEQA Guidelines
15183 (Projects Consistent with a Community Plan or Zoning). Pursuant to Public
Resources Code section 21083.3 and CEQA Guideline 15183(a), a project that is
consistent with the development densities established in a General Plan for which an EIR
was certified is not required to undergo additional environmental review “except as might
be necessary to examine whether there are project-specific significant effects which are
peculiar to the project or its site.” The project site is in the HD zone, which is consistent
with the High Density Residential General Plan land use designation. As there is no
development currently proposed for the subject site, there are no “project-specific
significant effects which are peculiar to the project or its site” to analyze at this time. Any
 future development applications on the subject site will be subject to project specific
CEQA review consistent with Public Resources Code Section 21083.3 and CEQA
Guidelines Section 15183 at the time a project is proposed to determine if mitigation would
be required to reduce potential impacts.

The final parcel map has been reviewed by the City’s contract surveyor, Meyer Land
Surveying, acting on behalf of the Public Works Department, and the map has been
deemed complete pursuant to Los Angeles County Municipal Code (LACMC) Section
21.16.040. The Subdivision Map Act requires the City Council to approve a final parcel
map if it substantially complies with a tentative parcel map approved by the Planning
Commission. (Government Code Section 66474.1) The City Council may deny approval
of the final map only for failure to meet or perform conditions applicable to the subdivision
at the time the tentative map was approved. Since the final parcel map is substantially
compliant with the previously approved tentative map, Staff is recommending that the City
Council approve final Parcel Map No. 084192.

map approval will expire.

recordation.

SECTION 1- FINDINGS

Tentative Parcel Map

The Planning Commission approves the Tentative Parcel Map based on the findings below:

  1. That the proposed map is consistent with the General Plan and applicable specific
  plans.

  The project is consistent with the City’s General Plan. The property has a General Plan
  land use designation of High Density Residential, which is consistent with the High
  Density Residential zoning designation. The subdivision of the project site is consistent
  with the applicable development standards of the designated zoning district. Therefore, the
  finding for denial cannot be made.

  2. That the design or improvement of the proposed map is consistent with the General
  Plan and applicable specific plans.

  No improvements are proposed as part of the project, including but not limited to grading,
  new construction, or addition to the existing residence. Therefore, the finding is not
  applicable to the project and a finding for denial cannot he made.

  3. That the site is physically suitable for the type of development.

  The project site is already developed with a single-family residence, which will be located
  on Parcel B of the proposed Tentative Parcel Map. There is no evidence to suggest that
  proposed Parcel A will be physically unsuitable for future residential development.
  Therefore, the finding for denial cannot be made.

  4. That the site is physically suitable for the proposed density of development.

  The project site is located within the High Density Residential zone, which permits density
  up to 40 dwelling units per acre (du/ac). There is no evidence to suggest that proposed
  Parcel A will be physically unsuitable for future residential development or will exceed
  allowable density for the zoning district. Therefore, the finding for denial cannot be made.

  5. That the design of the map or the proposed improvements are not likely to cause
  substantial environmental damage or substantially and avoidably injure fish or
  wildlife or their habitat.

  The project site is fully developed for the existing single-family residence and is identified
  as developed land in the Biotic Resources subsection of the General Plan (Figure TV-I,

  unlike that subdivision the site, which does not involve any development activities, will

6. That the design of the map or the type of improvements is not likely to cause serious

  No improvements are proposed as part of the project, including but not limited to grading,

SUBJECT:  Circuit Contract Amendment for COAST Program

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize City Staff to negotiate and execute the First
Amendment to the Professional Services Agreement between the City of Avalon and Circuit
Transit, Inc. for an additional not-to-exceed annual sum of $50,000.

REPORT SUMMARY: On March 5, 2024 the City Council authorized the City Manager to
negotiate and execute a contract agreement with Circuit Transit, Inc. (Circuit) to provide public
transportation services for a three-year period for a not to exceed annual sum of $725,000.

In June 2023, thanks to funding from the American Rescue Plan, the City had procured an all-
electric, zero emission fleet of vehicles to be used for public transportation. The fleet is
comprised of two (2) 2024 Ford eTransit vans and five (5) 2024 Polaris GEMs.

Though there are seven (7) vehicles in the public transit fleet, to provide service for 14 hours
each day, only two to three vehicles are on the street at any given time, allowing other vehicles
to charge and be ready to switch out midday.

Before the Circuit contract, the public transportation system in Avalon featured two (2) buses
that provided fixed route services and two (2) Dodge Mini-Vans that provided Dial-A-Ride
services. These services were sunset on March 31, 2024 and replaced by an on demand,
point-to-point system driven by a mobile app.

Since its launch, Circuit services  —  referred to as COAST (City of Avalon Seaside Transit)  —

have been immensely popular. Ridership has more than doubled and fare revenues are the
highest in the City’s public transit history. In addition to the increased ridership, Circuit services
are provided at a cost of almost 25% less than the previous public transit contractor.

Between the expenses associated with the contract costs, and the increased fare box revenue,
the City has experienced a $200,000 budget savings. This savings has reduced the amount
subsidized by the General Fund and allowed the City to allocate $100,000 in additional funding
to support the commuter subsidy program.

In the Fiscal Year 2024-25 Budget City Staff included $60,000 in the general fund to purchase
a new GEM to add to the public transit fleet. In lieu of purchasing a new vehicle, City Staff
 propose leasing up to two GEM vehicles from Circuit for $1,800 a month for a total, not to
exceed, annual sum of $50,000.

At this time, City Staff project to fully expend all of the available Local Return Funds (Prop A,
Prop C, Measure M, Measure R, Prop A Discretionary, and TDA 8) designated for land transit
operations. Though the City’s program expenses and revenues are positive, current Local
Return Fund estimates are below projections. If there is a shift in projections, the lease of
transit vehicles is a reimbursable expense eligible to be paid by Local Return Funds already
allocated to land transit operations. In this Fiscal Year, a capital outlay for a vehicle purchase
cannot be reimbursed through Local Return Funds; however, City Staff may request to modify
the budget in the next cycle to allow for a capital outlay.

At the current rate of wear and tear, City Staff believe that leasing vehicles makes economic
sense. Due to the Island’s topography, condition of roadways, and the hours the transit fleet is
in use, City Mechanics anticipate the City may need to begin replacing vehicles on three to five
year cycles.

City Staff recommend the City Council authorizes the City Manager to execute the First
Amendment to the Professional Services Agreement with Circuit for a not to exceed additional
$50,000 annually to support the lease of up to two (2) additional GEMs. These vehicles will be
used to supplement operations and grow the transit program.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Public health and fiscal responsibility.

FISCAL IMPACTS: If approved, the expense may be eligible to be paid by grant funds
already allocated to the local transit system.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: No additional
vehicles will be added to the City’s COAST fleet.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Implement City Council direction.

REPORT SUMMARY: On November 25, 2024 the City of Avalon issued a notice to
proceed to Jordahl Construction, Inc. to complete the Five Corners Site Improvement
Project (CIP Project #1 80003).

Knowing a portion of the scope of work essential for this project was being completed in

services and sediment screening as well as a final monitoring report for a total of

City Staff met with Montrose to discuss the proposal and project scope on January 16,
2025 and developed a plan to mitigate project costs while ensuring preservation and
protection of culturally significant items discovered on site.

into a professional services agreement with Montrose Environmental Services, Inc. to
provide cultural resource consulting for the Five Corners Site Improvement Project for a
not to exceed sum of $118,000.
 On April 17, 2025, Montrose provided City Staff with Change Order #1. This change order
request expands Montrose’s monitoring time on site until May 2025. Initially, monitoring
efforts were projected to continue from December 2024 through the end of March 2025.

area, Montrose and City Staff see the need to expand the site monitoring through May
2025.

#1 to the existing professional services agreement with Montrose Environmental

Improvement Project, for an additional sum of $47,466 for a new total contract sum of

To Whom It May Concern:

On behalf of Mandeville Modular, we are pleased to present our proposal for the development
of the Civic Center Housing Development, a critical initiative aimed at addressing the pressing
issue of affordable housing in the City of San Avalon. This project represents a significant
opportunity to leverage our expertise in modular building services to create a housing facility
that will provide affordable housing options in the community.

The Civic Center Housing Project in Avalon, California, represents a pivotal initiative aimed at
addressing the critical housing challenges faced by the City of Ava Ion. Situated on the
picturesque Catalina Island, Avalon is a unique community with a vibrant tourist-based
economy and a strong commitment to environmental sustainability. However, its remote
island location, 22 miles off the coast of Southern California, presents significant hurdles in
terms of housing affordability and availability, particularly for the essential workforce that
supports the city’s operations and services.

The Civic Center Housing Project is strategically designed to mitigate these housing challenges
by developing a 3-story, 22-unit modular housing complex on the City Hall Campus land at 410
Avalon Canyon Road. This project is integral to the City’s efforts to provide both temporary
and long-term housing solutions for its essential workforce, thereby improving employee
recruitment and retention. The project aligns with Avalon’s broader goals of creating a
sustainable, model community that balances economic vitality with environmental stewardship.

In addition, due to Avalon’s unique geographic and environmental context necessitates, a
tailored approach to the Civic Center Housing Project. The island’s limited land availability and

A Sustainable Practice
We design sustainable projects to affirm our commitment to conserve
resources today and leave the world a better place for tomorrow. Our
approach is informed by an understanding of economic and environmental
impacts, and efficient natural resource utilization. We focus on integrating
natural systems rather than developing costly solutions that eventually
become economically inefficient.

Similar to our belief that good design does not have to be associated
with high costs, meeting sustainable goals can be cost-effective when
planned accordingly.

The critical piece of having a sustainable practice and project within
budget is to have this thinking from the beginning. With a clear green
goal in mind from the start, the design team can form the project to
take advantage of many sustainable features that require little to no
cost. Starting with passive strategies tuned to the local microclimatic
conditions and incorporating baseline specifications, such as no-VOC
products and demolition recycling, the project team can more easily
meet a client’s sustainability goals with little additional effort.

Our experience with California projects under the strictest energy code
in the country has made sustainable design a baseline part of our practice.
Reducing our carbon footprint is one of the most pressing issues of the
building industry in the 21st century, and our awareness of its seriousness
colors all our decisions. As a firm that is continuously looking for new
ways to approach building, such as factory-built housing, we are always
looking for ways to be more efficient and leverage technology to get us
there.

Whenever possible, we utilize the LEED rating system to design.
construct, renovate, and operate existing and new facilities as well as new
construction. Our multi-sector experience allows us to have a wide-range
understanding in greenhouse gas reduction strategies. green buildings,
and energy technologies.

when partnering with subconsultants. we lean on those who have a

REPORT SUMMARY: On October 2, 2024, the City released a Request for Proposals
from qualified venders to provide building, planning and engineering consultant services.
The City received six proposals by the stated deadline including a proposal from
International Consulting Services, Inc. (ICS).

On December 17, 2024 the City Council awarded a contract to 4Leaf, Inc. to provide
Building Division Services. However, within the staff report City Staff advised that they
may return to City Council to make recommendations for additional on-call contracts to
support Planning and the Public Works Department.

At this time, ICS works as a sub-consultant for ESG, Engineering, Inc (ESG). ESG is
contracted to provide on-call engineering services to the City. On April 15, 2025, the City
Council approved a new contract with ESG to continue to provide on-call engineering
services through December 2028 for an annual contract sum not to exceed $800,000.

ICS is currently engaged with City Staff on a number of complex CIP projects. Due to the
level of nuance and the timing of these projects, City Staff believe there will be no
competitive advantage to bidding the on-call project management services contract at this
time. Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) Section 3-4.111 (c) outlines an exception from
bidding and other competitive procedures for economic efficiency. Per the AMC:

  If a competitive market does not exist, or the City will not gain a competitive
  advantage by using the formal contract bid or other competitive procedure, or
  where the public project, goods or seivices may be obtained more economically or
  efficiently without the procedure, the City may dispense with formal bidding or other
  competitive procedures.
 ICS performs high level project management support for the Workforce Housing and
Cabrillo Mole Rehabilitation Phase II Projects as a sub-consultant. By contracting directly
with ICS, the City anticipates a significant cost savings from the mark-up provided for their
services when contracted through ESG.

Task orders for on-call services will be driven by the approved budget. Annually funds
cannot be spent unless they are a part of an approved, budgeted, project or account or
receive additional City Council approval in accordance with the approved budget and
fiscal policies of the budget. Task orders related to grant funds may be eligible for
reimbursement or payment through grants, and will be accounted for in the grant project’s
budget.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Not to exceed $100,000 for all task orders per fiscal year for all
approved on-call engineer services for a contract of three years. Funding will be allocated
to the appropriate budgeted project.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Improved project management processes.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City will not
efficiently contract project management resources for current and future capital projects.

  a.  CONSTRUCTION MANAGEMENT SERVICES

  Construction management involves process of planning, coordination, and control
  of construction projects from inception to completion. The primary goal of
  construction management is to ensure that a project is completed on time, within
  budget, and to the specified quality standards.

  To achieve this goal, we see our roles and responsibilities as follows:

  i.  Project Planning: Developing a clear roadmap for the project, including
  timelines, resource allocation, and budgeting

  ii.  Cost Management: Estimating costs, managing budgets, and ensuring
  financial efficiency throughout the project lifecycle

  iii.  Scheduling: Creating and maintaining a project schedule that outlines the
  timeline for various phases of the construction process.

  iv.  Project Management & Communication: Coordinating between various
  stakeholders, including clients, architects, engineers, subcontractors, and
  suppliers to ensure project deadlines and goals are met and or implement
  adjustments when needed. We anticipate that CS will be participating in

  v.  Risk Management: Identifying potential risks and developing strategies to

  vi.  Quality Control: Implementing processes to ensure that the construction

  vii.  Safety Management: Ensuring that construction practices comply with

  viii.  Contract Administration: Managing contracts with stakeholders and

  Coordination document control processes and procedures. Frequent

  PROJECT UNDERSTANDING

  Section 3.5.1 of the Avalon Wastewater Treatment Facility discharge permit (Order R4-2024-
  0253) requires the City submit a Climate Change Effects Vulnerability Assessment and
  Management Plan (Climate Change Plan). Section 6.3.4 of the permit has more specific
  requirements of this plan: Climate Change Effects Vulnerability Assessment and Mitigation
  Plan:
  The Discharger shall consider the impacts of climate change as they affect the
  operation of the treatment facility due to flooding, wildfires, or other climate related
  changes. The Discharger shall develop a Climate Change Effects Vulnerability
  Assessment and Mitigation Plan (Climate Change Plan) to assess and manage climate
  change-related effects that may impact the waste water treatment facility’s
  operation, water supplies, its collection system, and water quality, including any
  projected changes to the influent water temperature and pollutant concentrations,
  and beneficial uses. The permittee shall also identify new or increased threats to the
  sewer system resulting from climate change that may impact desired levels of service
  in the next 50 years. The permittee shall project upgrades to existing assets or new
  infrastructure projects, and associated costs, necessary to meet desired levels of
  service. Climate change research also indicates the overarching driver of climate
  change is increased atmospheric carbon dioxide from human activity. The increased
  carbon dioxide emissions trigger changes to climatic patterns, which increase the
  intensity of sea level rise and coastal storm surges, lead to more erratic rainfall and
  local weather patterns, trigger a gradual warming of freshwater and ocean
  temperatures, and trigger changes to ocean water chemistry. As such, the Climate
  Change Plan shall also identify steps being taken or planned to address greenhouse
  gas emissions attributable to wastewater treatment plants, solids handling, and
  effluent discharge processes. The Climate Change Plan is due 12 months after
  effective date of this Order.

  PERC has requested a proposal to prepare a Climate Change Plan following the PRISM Model
  which is acceptable to the Los Angeles Regional Water Quality Control Board.

BACKGROUND
In Southern California, the predicted impacts of climate change are numerous. Annual average
temperatures are expected to increase, coupled with a higher frequency of extreme heat days. A
likely consequence of this warmer climate will be more severe drought periods, leading to an
increase in the amount and intensity of fires and a longer fire season.

In addition, precipitation patterns are likely to be modified. A decrease in snowfall, combined with
warmer temperatures, will induce a decrease in the amount and duration of snowpack, an essential
source of freshwater to the region. Although changes to mean precipitation are expected to be small,
the increasing occurrence of extreme precipitation events will amplify the risk of flooding. These
impacts may affect water quality in multiple ways, including decreases in stream flow, reductions
in, and changes to, aquatic habitats, increases in surface water temperature, increases in pollutant
levels, sedimentation, algal growth, and changes in salinity levels and acidification in coastal areas.

For permitted facilities and for facilities applying for a new or renewed permit, such as Publicly Owned
Treatment Works (POTWs), specific impacts could include, but are not limited to, an increase in
the concentration of pollutants entering the facility, an increase in the temperature of effluents and
receiving waters, an increase in storm water inflow and infiltration, increase in flooding
inundation of facilities, sewer overflows, power outages, pump maintenance issues, and onsite or
nearby hillside destabilization.

On March 7, 2017, the State Water Board adopted Resolution No. 2017-0012, Comprehensive
Response to Climate Change, responding to the challenges posed by climate change and requiring
a proactive approach to climate change in all State Water Board actions, including drinking water
regulation, water quality protection, and financial assistance.

On May 10, 201 8, the Los Angeles Water Board adopted Resolution No. RI 8-004, A Resolution to
Prioritize Actions to Adapt to and Mitigate the Impacts of Climate Change on the Los Angeles
Region ‘s Water Resources and Associated Beneficial Uses.

The resolution summarizes the steps taken to date to address the impacts of climate change within
the Los Angeles Water Board’s programs, and lists a series of additional steps, including the
identification of potential regulatory adaptation and mitigation measures that could be implemented
on a short-term and long-term basis by each of the Los Angeles Water Board’s programs to mitigate
the effects of climate change on water resources and associated beneficial uses where possible.

INTRODUCTION
For Publicly Owned Treatment Works (POTW5) in California, renewing an NPDES permit now
requires the development of a Climate Change Effects Vulnerability Assessment and Mitigation
Plan (Climate Change Plan) to assess and manage climate change-related effects that may impact
the wastewater treatment facility’s operation, water supplies, its collection system, and water
quality, including any projected changes to the influent water temperature and pollutant
concentrations, and beneficial uses.

POTWs are required to consider the impacts of climate change as they affect the operation of the
treatment facility due to flooding, wildfire, or other climate-related changes. POTWs are also
required to identify new or increased threats to the sewer system resulting from climate change
that may impact desired levels of service in the next 50 years. In addition, POTWs are required
to project upgrades to existing assets or new infrastructure projects, and associated costs,
necessary to meet desired levels of service.

Climate change research also indicates the overarching driver of climate change is increased
atmospheric carbon dioxide from human activity. The increased carbon dioxide emissions trigger
changes to climatic patterns, which increase the intensity of sea level rise and coastal storm
surges, lead to more erratic rainfall and local weather patterns, trigger a gradual warming of
freshwater and ocean temperatures, and trigger changes to ocean water chemistry. As such, the
Climate Change Plan shall also identify steps being taken or planned to address greenhouse gas
emissions attributable to wastewater treatment plants, solids handling, and effluent discharge
processes.

  In considering the impacts of climate change, representative concentration pathways (RCP) will
  be used. RCP are climate change scenarios to project future greenhouse gas concentrations.
  These pathways (or trajectories) describe future greenhouse gas concentrations (not emissions)
  and have been formally adopted by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
  The pathways describe different climate change scenarios, all of which were considered possible
  depending on the amount of greenhouse gases (GHG) emitted in the years to come. The four
  RCPs  — originally RCP2.6, RCP4.5, RCP6, and RCP8.5  —are labelled after the expected
  changes in radiative forcing from the year 1750 to the year 2100 (2.6, 4.5, 6, and 8.5 W/m2.
  respectively). The IPCC Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) began to use these four pathways for
